label: Homology As A Machine
notes: Start with homology as a machine rather than as a list of examples. The inputs are cells or simplices, the gears are boundary maps, and the output remembers cycles that cannot be explained as boundaries. Name the quotient formula early because every later construction preserves that pattern.

label: Why Chains Replace Loops
notes: Use the ladder to motivate chains as a more flexible language than loops alone. A zero-cell creates a component, a one-cell can create a loop, and a two-cell can kill that loop by making it a boundary. Higher cells repeat the same create or kill logic.

label: Chain Complexes
notes: Emphasize that the algebraic object is the whole sequence, not a single group. The condition boundary after boundary equals zero is the structural guarantee that boundaries are automatically cycles, so the quotient defining homology is meaningful rather than a lucky accident.

label: Cycles Modulo Boundaries
notes: Read the left picture as a loop with no filled disk available and the right picture as the same loop after a two-cell has been attached. The difference is not whether the path closes; both close. The difference is whether it bounds a higher-dimensional chain.

label: Delta-Complex Surface Models
notes: The surface quotient artifact is a compact way to see why presentations matter. A torus model has Euler characteristic zero and first homology rank two, while the projective-plane model has a degree two boundary map that leaves a torsion class rather than a free generator.

label: Boundary Signs
notes: Spend time on the alternating signs because they are the first place orientation enters the algebra. The triangle boundary has three directed edges, and applying the next boundary cancels every vertex contribution in pairs. That cancellation is the concrete face of boundary squared zero.

label: Singular Homology
notes: Move from triangulated or cellular models to arbitrary spaces by allowing every continuous simplex map into the space. This creates a huge chain group, but the boundary is still computed on the faces of the standard simplex, which is why functoriality is available.

label: Homotopy Invariance
notes: Present the prism as an organized chain homotopy. A homotopy between maps sweeps each simplex through a prism, and the prism identity says the two induced chain maps differ by a boundary-level correction. Therefore they induce the same map on homology.

label: Exactness And Relative Homology
notes: Use the exact-sequence machine to make relative homology feel operational. The phrase image equals kernel means every class that dies at the next station was already produced by the previous station. Relative groups measure what remains after the subspace is collapsed out of the calculation.

label: Long Exact Sequence Of A Pair
notes: The connecting homomorphism is the star of this slide. A relative n-cycle may have a boundary that lies inside A, and that boundary becomes a class one degree lower in A. This is the algebraic bookkeeping behind attaching-cell computations.

label: Excision By Subdivision
notes: Excision looks mysterious until subdivision enters. Name the hypothesis explicitly: take U inside A with closure contained in the interior of A, so removing U from both X and A induces the same relative homology. Repeated barycentric subdivision makes simplices small enough to lie inside the chosen cover, and the check artifact marks step three as the first good subdivision.

label: Degree And Local Degree
notes: Degree is homology of top-dimensional spheres turned into an integer. Local degree decomposes the global count into signed preimage contributions, which explains why reflection has degree negative one, a constant map has degree zero, and composition multiplies degrees.

label: Cellular Homology
notes: Cellular homology is the computational payoff of homotopy invariance and excision. The chain group has one generator per cell, and the boundary coefficient is the degree of the attaching map onto a lower cell. This compresses many singular chains into a small matrix.

label: Worked Cellular Examples
notes: Use the table as a quick matrix-reading drill. S1 and S2 have zero cellular differentials in the displayed dimensions, while RP2 and the Moore space have one nontrivial attaching degree. The integer two or three is exactly what becomes torsion in first homology.

label: Euler Characteristic
notes: Euler characteristic is the alternating trace left after the chain complex cancels boundaries against cycles. For finite CW complexes, the alternating cell count agrees with the alternating Betti count. It is not a complete invariant, but it is a fast consistency check for computations.

label: Mayer-Vietoris
notes: Describe Mayer-Vietoris as exactness for a union. The intersection term prevents double-counting, the direct sum records the two pieces separately, and the connecting arrow detects cycles that become visible only after gluing. The same image-kernel rule drives the sequence.

label: Coefficients And Torsion
notes: Changing coefficients is not cosmetic. Tensoring with a field can erase torsion or reveal it when the field characteristic matches the attaching degree. The RP2 and Moore examples are useful because the same spaces switch rank depending on Q, F2, or F3.

label: H1 And Abelianization
notes: First homology is the abelian shadow of the fundamental group. Commutators vanish because chains add without remembering word order, so H1 keeps the loop classes that survive after forcing multiplication to commute. The genus two check gives rank four, matching four standard generators.

label: Applications And Recap
notes: Close by pointing out that the chapter's applications are not separate tricks. Degree arguments, fixed-point results, surface calculations, and coefficient tests all use the same chain machine: choose a model, compute boundaries, pass to cycles modulo boundaries, and interpret functorial consequences.
